title: Evolve Life with a stable source generation
audience: Students with basic programming knowledge who are new to assembly
learningObjectives: Use padded dead halos and distinguish row strides
Separate source reads from destination writes and exchange roles
Publish and verify complete generations through a public checkpoint
Explain local coverage, boundary conditions, and instruction-count comparisons

steps.title: Read the local update rule

quiz.prompt: Is the center included in its own neighbor count?

choices.text: Yes, always.
No; only the eight surrounding cells count.
Only at the edge.

hints.text: Separate the current cell from the neighbor sum.
A dead center with two neighbors stays dead; a live center with two survives.

steps.title: Keep one generation stable while computing the next

quiz.prompt: Why use a separate destination?

choices.text: To keep earlier writes from changing later neighbor reads.
To double every neighbor count.
To change the rule on alternate rows.

hints.text: Ask which generation each byte belongs to at the moment it is read.
Changing traversal order must not change a completed generation.

steps.title: Distinguish the three row strides

quiz.prompt: Which stride belongs to a padded working board?

choices.text: Eight words.
Thirty-two bytes.
Ten bytes.

hints.text: Include both halo columns when counting a physical row.
Working interior (0,0) is at offset eleven; framebuffer (0,0) is at offset zero.

steps.title: Load current and destination pointers

quiz.prompt: What does a requested count of two mean?

choices.text: Display only generations one and two.
Initialize generation zero, then evolve twice.
Copy the seed twice without evolving.

hints.text: Count transitions separately from the initial state.
`$s0` identifies `board_a`, `$s1` `board_b`, `$s2` is the requested count, and `$s3` is zero.

steps.title: Prepare to copy the seed interior

quiz.prompt: Why is the first destination not `board_a` itself?

choices.text: Offset zero is part of the dead halo.
The first eleven cells are always alive.
The board is word-addressed.

hints.text: Locate physical row zero and column zero on the halo diagram.
The input cursor starts at seed and the destination cursor at `board_a`+11.

steps.title: Copy one binary byte

quiz.prompt: Does `lbu` create a live link to the seed byte?

choices.text: Yes, later stores update the register automatically.
Only if the byte is one.
No; it copies the current byte value into a register.

hints.text: A register holds a value, not a subscription to memory.
Only the first interior byte has been copied at this partial stage.

steps.title: Close the copy loops and skip halo columns

quiz.prompt: Why add two only to the working-board cursor?

choices.text: The seed rows also contain two hidden cells.
Only the padded representation has halo columns.
Two is the live-cell color.

hints.text: Compare the eight-byte and ten-byte physical row strides.
At `seed_copied`, all 64 interior bytes equal the seed; halos remain zero.

steps.title: Observe initialized generation zero

quiz.prompt: Which board is current before any swap?

choices.text: `board_a`.
`board_b`.
Neither; the seed allocation is writable current state.

hints.text: Follow the initial current-pointer assignment.
The default live cells are (2,3), (3,3), and (4,3).

quiz.prompt: How far should the output cursor move after one cell?

choices.text: One byte.
Ten bytes.
Four bytes.

hints.text: Each display cell is a word, even though each simulation cell is a byte.
The renderer has independent source and frame cursors.

choices.text: Zero terminates every program.
A previous live pixel must be erased.

hints.text: The frame may contain an earlier generation or arbitrary initial words.
The first default cell is black; no other frame cell has been rendered at this partial stage.

choices.text: After the complete frame and generation word agree with the current board.
After computing just the first row.
Whenever the destination pointer changes.

hints.text: Publication describes a completed state, not progress inside a cell loop.
At the first ready checkpoint, generation is zero and the frame shows the seed.

Only after the first evolved board.

hints.text: The initial board still needs to be displayed for a zero-step request.

steps.title: Address matching source and destination cells

hints.text: The allocations differ; their layouts agree.

steps.title: Count exactly eight source neighbors

quiz.prompt: Why does a corner need no special load branch?

choices.text: Its off-board neighbors are represented by zero halo bytes.
Corners always have eight live neighbors.
The simulator ignores invalid memory reads.

hints.text: Translate the corner into padded coordinates before applying offsets.
At the first default cell, the neighbor count is zero. Every read remains within the padded allocation.

steps.title: Evaluate birth or survival with Boolean values

quiz.prompt: When does a dead cell with two neighbors become alive?

choices.text: Always.
Only on even generations.
Never under this rule.

hints.text: The two-neighbor term must include the current alive bit.
`$t4` is exactly zero or one, the state to write into the destination.

steps.title: Store the next state into the other board

quiz.prompt: Is this partial destination ready to render as a generation?

choices.text: Yes, because one cell is correct.
No; all 64 next-state cells must be complete first.
Only if the first cell is dead.

hints.text: Distinguish a cell boundary from a generation boundary.
The first next-state cell is complete; the rest of the destination may still contain old data.

steps.title: Complete all rows before changing roles

quiz.prompt: Which board supplied every neighbor in this sweep?

choices.text: The unchanged current board.
Whichever byte was written most recently.
The framebuffer.

hints.text: Follow the base used for all `lbu` neighbor addresses.
At `generation_computed`, the destination is complete and the current board is still the old generation.

quiz.prompt: What does a complete destination alone establish?

It changes two addresses instead of moving one hundred bytes.

hints.text: Count what is written by the three move instructions.

quiz.prompt: Why reuse the renderer after swapping?

The frame automatically follows pointer assignments.
It recalculates neighbors as part of every pixel store.

hints.text: Separate model evolution from color conversion.

quiz.prompt: Does generation two matching generation zero prove that no evolution occurred?

Only for a white frame.

hints.text: A repeated final pattern can hide a skipped transition.

hints.text: Boundary conditions are part of the model, not an address-calculation convenience alone.
